cover.title: 50 API Interview Questions
cover.subtitle: Backend & SDE Handbook
cover.tagline: For backend and SDE candidates: 50 questions on 14 themed pages, each with a short answer, key points and a visual, ordered from fundamentals to scenarios

blocks.q: Q1. What is a REST API and what are its architectural constraints?
a_bullets: REST is an ==architectural style== acting on resources via URLs and HTTP methods.
Resources are nouns: `/users/7`
Server sends JSON representations
Six constraints; last is optional

blocks.q: Q2. What is the difference between REST and SOAP?
a_bullets: REST is a lightweight ==style== over HTTP, SOAP a strict XML ==protocol==.
REST allows JSON, XML or text
SOAP needs XML envelopes, WSDL
SOAP has built-in WS-Security

blocks.q: Q3. What does it mean for an API to be stateless, and why does it matter?
a_bullets: Stateless means the server stores ==no client session==; every request is self-contained.
Auth token travels with each call
Any server instance can answer
Scaling and failover are simple

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: REST: resources, verbs, ==stateless== calls. SOAP: strict XML. Stateless eases scaling.

blocks.q: Q4. What is the difference between PUT and PATCH?
a_bullets: ==PUT== replaces the whole resource, while ==PATCH== changes only the fields you send.
PUT: send the **full** representation
PATCH: send only the changed fields
Omitted fields in PUT reset to defaults

blocks.q: Q5. What is the difference between POST and PUT?
a_bullets: ==POST== creates a resource where the server picks the URI; ==PUT== writes to a URI the client names.
POST repeated creates duplicates
PUT repeated leaves the same end state
PUT creates or replaces at a known URL

blocks.q: Q6. Which HTTP methods are safe and which are idempotent?
a_bullets: A ==safe== method never changes server state; an ==idempotent== one gives the same end state when repeated.
Safe means read-only: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS
Every safe method is also idempotent
DELETE is idempotent but not safe

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: PUT replaces, PATCH edits, POST creates. Only GET, HEAD and OPTIONS are safe; POST is never idempotent.

blocks.q: Q7. What is the difference between 401 and 403?
a_bullets: **401** means the server does not know who you are; **403** means it knows you but refuses access.
401: missing, expired or invalid credentials.
403: valid identity, but no permission for this resource.
Retry 401 after logging in; retrying 403 changes nothing.

blocks.q: Q8. What is the difference between 400, 422 and 409?
a_bullets: **400** is a malformed request, **422** is well-formed but invalid, **409** clashes with current server state.
400: broken JSON or a bad query parameter.
422: parses fine, fails validation (email invalid).
409: duplicate username or stale version update.

blocks.q: Q9. When do you return 200, 201, 202 and 204?
a_bullets: Pick the code by outcome: ==200== done with a body, ==201== created, ==202== accepted for later, ==204== done with no body.
201 should carry a `Location` header for the new resource.
202 means work is queued; give a status URL to poll.
204 suits DELETE and PUT with nothing to return.

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: 401 = who are you? 403 = not allowed. 400 = broken, 422 = invalid, 409 = conflict. 201 creates, 202 queues, 204 is empty.

blocks.q: Q10. What is content negotiation and which headers drive it?
a_bullets: The client lists the formats it can accept, and the server picks the best matching ==representation==.
`Accept`, `Accept-Language` and `Accept-Encoding` carry the preferences.
Server replies with `Content-Type`, or **406** if nothing fits.
`Vary` tells caches which headers shaped the response.

blocks.q: Q11. What is the difference between Cache-Control, ETag and Last-Modified?
a_bullets: `Cache-Control` sets how long a response stays ==fresh==, while `ETag` and `Last-Modified` let the client ==revalidate== it cheaply.
`max-age=3600` skips the network for an hour.
`ETag` fingerprints content; match returns **304**, no body.
`Last-Modified` is a timestamp with one-second precision.

blocks.q: Q12. What happens in an HTTP request from browser to server and back?
a_bullets: The browser resolves the host, opens a secure connection, sends the request, and renders the server's response.
DNS turns the hostname into an IP address.
TCP and TLS handshakes precede the first request byte.
Server routes, runs logic, returns status, headers, body.

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: Accept picks the format, Vary keeps caches honest, max-age skips the network, ETag revalidates with a 304.

blocks.q: Q13. What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
a_bullets: AuthN proves **who**; authZ decides **what** they may do.
AuthN first, authZ every request
Failed authN `401`, authZ `403`
Roles and scopes drive authZ

blocks.q: Q14. What is the difference between session-based and token-based authentication?
a_bullets: Sessions keep state on the **server**; tokens carry signed state.
Session: cookie holds only an ID
Token: signature verified, no lookup
Tokens scale; sessions share storage

blocks.q: Q15. What are API keys and when are they enough?
a_bullets: An API key is a random string identifying the **application**, not a user.
Enough: server-to-server, public reads
Not enough: per-user identity, consent
Send in header, store hashed, rotate

slides.subtitle: Who are you, what can you do

blocks.q: Q16. How does a JWT work and what are its three parts?
a_bullets: A ==JWT== is a signed token: `header.payload.signature`, base64url-encoded.
Header names the algorithm, e.g. **RS256**.
Payload holds claims: `sub`, `exp`, `iss`, roles.
Signature proves integrity; payload is **not** secret.

blocks.q: Q17. How do you handle JWT expiry, refresh tokens and revocation?
a_bullets: Issue ==short-lived== access tokens plus a rotating refresh token; denylist `jti` to revoke.
Rotate refresh token each use; reuse means theft.
Store refresh tokens hashed, server-side, httpOnly cookies.
Keep denylisted `jti` in Redis until `exp`.

blocks.q: Q18. What are the OAuth 2.0 grant types and when is each used?
a_bullets: A grant is how a client gets a token; choose by ==client type== and user presence.
Auth Code with **PKCE** is the default for logins.
Implicit and password grants are deprecated.
Client credentials: no user, only a service.

blocks.q: Q19. What is the difference between OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect?
a_bullets: OAuth 2.0 handles ==authorization==; OpenID Connect adds ==authentication== via an ID token.
OAuth issues access tokens: what the app may do.
OIDC adds an ID token (JWT) and `openid` scope.
UserInfo endpoint returns profile claims.

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: JWT is signed, not encrypted. Short access tokens, rotating refresh tokens. Auth Code + PKCE for users. OAuth: what; OIDC: who.

blocks.q: Q20. What is CORS and how does a preflight request work?
a_bullets: ==CORS== lets a server say which origins may read its responses.
Browser sends `OPTIONS` preflight before risky calls
Server replies with `Access-Control-Allow-*` headers
**Never** pair `*` origin with credentials

blocks.q: Q21. How do you protect an API from SQL injection, XSS and CSRF?
a_bullets: Treat input as hostile: ==parameterize== queries, encode output, verify intent.
SQLi: prepared statements, no concatenation
XSS: escape output, set CSP header
CSRF: SameSite cookies, anti-forgery tokens

blocks.q: Q22. What is the OWASP API Security Top 10 and which risks matter most?
a_bullets: The ==OWASP API Top 10== ranks the most common, damaging API flaws.
**Broken** object/function-level authorization lead
Broken authentication, excessive data exposure follow
Also: no rate limits, misconfig, SSRF

blocks.q: Q23. What is BOLA/IDOR and how do you prevent it?
a_bullets: ==BOLA== (IDOR) means reading another user's object by changing its ID.
Check **ownership** on every access, server-side
UUIDs are only extra defence
Never trust client-sent IDs

blocks.q: Q24. What is the difference between offset and cursor pagination?
a_bullets: ==Offset== skips N rows by position, while ==cursor== resumes after the last item you saw.
Offset allows jumping to any page number
Cursor stays stable when rows change
Cursor only moves next or previous

blocks.q: Q25. Why does offset pagination get slow on large tables?
a_bullets: The database must read and **discard** every skipped row before returning yours.
Cost grows linearly with the offset
Page 5000 scans 100k rows for 20
Keyset `WHERE` uses the index instead

blocks.q: Q26. How do you design filtering, sorting and field selection in a REST API?
a_bullets: Use ==query parameters== on the collection, with a whitelist of allowed fields.
Filter by field name: `status=paid`
Sort with a prefix: `-` means descending
Select columns with `fields=` to cut payload

blocks.q: Q27. How do you paginate a feed where new items are inserted constantly?
a_bullets: Use ==cursor== (keyset) pagination on a stable sort, so inserts never shift your place.
Sort by `created_at` plus `id` tie-breaker
Offset would repeat or skip items
Return an opaque `next_cursor` token
example_code: ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: Offset is simple but slow and unstable; cursor is fast and stable. Whitelist filters, and always sort with a unique tie-breaker.

blocks.q: Q28. How does rate limiting work and why is it needed?
a_bullets: A limiter counts requests per client key, rejecting those over quota.
Stops abuse, brute-force, scraping
Noisy tenant can't starve others
Caps cost, protects database

blocks.q: Q29. What is the difference between token bucket, leaky bucket and sliding window?
a_bullets: They differ in counting: bursts, smoothing, or rolling total.
==Token bucket== refills steadily, allows bursts
==Leaky bucket== drains at fixed rate
==Sliding window== counts exact last N seconds

blocks.q: Q30. How do you implement distributed rate limiting across servers?
a_bullets: Keep counters in one shared store, usually Redis.
Atomic check-and-increment via Lua
TTL expires old windows
Or enforce once at gateway

blocks.q: Q31. What does a 429 response look like and how should clients react?
a_bullets: Server returns 429 Too Many Requests, usually with Retry-After.
Wait for Retry-After first
Else exponential backoff with jitter
Never retry in tight loop

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: Limit per key or user, not IP (shared NAT). Token bucket, Redis, 429 + Retry-After.

blocks.q: Q32. What are the layers where an API response can be cached?
a_bullets: A response can be cached at ==every hop== between the client and the database, and the closer to the user the cheaper the hit.
Client: browser or app, via `Cache-Control`
Edge: CDN near the user, shared by all
Server: Redis or in-memory, before the DB

blocks.q: Q33. How do you invalidate a cache and keep it consistent?
a_bullets: Pick a ==TTL== for bounded staleness, and add **explicit** invalidation when data must be fresh.
Cache-aside: write DB, then delete the key
Versioned keys or URLs skip purging entirely
Stale-while-revalidate hides refresh latency

blocks.q: Q34. What does an API gateway do and when do you need one?
a_bullets: A gateway is the ==single entry point== that handles cross-cutting concerns before requests reach services.
Auth, rate limiting, routing, TLS termination
Also request logging and response aggregation
Needed with many services or many client types

blocks.q: Q35. What is the difference between an API gateway, reverse proxy and load balancer?
a_bullets: They overlap, but each is defined by its ==main job==: API logic, forwarding, or spreading traffic.
Gateway is a reverse proxy plus API features
Load balancer only picks a healthy backend
Real products often combine all three roles

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: Cache close to the user, expire with a **TTL**, delete on write, and let the gateway own auth and limits.

blocks.q: Q36. What is idempotency and how do you make a POST idempotent?
a_bullets: An operation is ==idempotent== if repeating it leaves the same end state as doing it once.
POST is not idempotent by default; add a client-sent key.
Client sends a unique `Idempotency-Key` header per action.
Server stores key plus response, replays it on repeat.

blocks.q: Q37. How do you prevent duplicate payments when a client retries?
a_bullets: Save every request's idempotency key with a **unique** constraint, and return the stored result on a repeat.
Make the key insert atomic, before charging anything.
Same key, different body: reject with 422.
Expire keys after about 24 hours.

blocks.q: Q38. What is the difference between webhooks and polling?
a_bullets: Polling means the client asks repeatedly; a ==webhook== means the server pushes an HTTP POST when an event happens.
Polling wastes calls and adds delay up to the interval.
Webhooks are near real-time and cheap for the sender.
Webhooks need a public endpoint and failure handling.

blocks.q: Q39. How do you design reliable and secure webhook delivery?
a_bullets: Sign each payload, retry failures with backoff, and make receivers idempotent by event id.
Sign the body with **HMAC-SHA256** and a timestamp.
Receiver returns 2xx fast, then processes async.
Retry with exponential backoff, then dead-letter queue.

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: Idempotency key + unique constraint = safe retries. Webhooks: sign it, ack fast, retry, dedupe.

blocks.q: Q40. What are the ways to version an API and which do you prefer?
a_bullets: Version in the ==URI path==, a ==header== or a ==query param==; I prefer the path for visibility.
**Path**: /v1/users, easy to route, cache and debug
**Header**: Accept vnd.api.v2+json keeps URLs clean but hides version
**Query**: ?version=2 is simple but easy to forget

blocks.q: Q41. How do you make API changes without breaking existing clients?
a_bullets: Make only ==additive== changes, and run old and new versions side by side during a deprecation window.
Add optional fields; never remove, rename or retype
Clients ignore unknown fields (tolerant reader)
Announce with `Deprecation` and `Sunset` headers

blocks.q: Q42. How do you design file uploads for large files?
a_bullets: Let the client upload ==directly to object storage== in resumable chunks, using a pre-signed URL.
Multipart chunks let a failed part retry alone
Pre-signed URLs keep big bytes off your API servers
Verify a checksum, then confirm the upload is complete

blocks.q: Q43. How do you design a consistent API error response format?
a_bullets: Return one ==error envelope== everywhere, ideally RFC 9457 `application/problem+json`.
Correct HTTP status plus a stable machine-readable code
Human message for developers, never stack traces
Include a request ID so support can trace it

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: Version in the path, only add never break, upload via pre-signed chunks, and return one problem+json error shape.

blocks.q: Q44. How do you test an API: unit, integration, contract and load tests?
a_bullets: Stack four layers: many fast tests below, few slow ones on top.
==Unit==: one handler, mocked DB, milliseconds
==Integration==: real DB and routes, checks status/body
==Contract==: schema agreed; ==load==: p95 under traffic

blocks.q: Q45. Which metrics and logs do you monitor for an API in production?
a_bullets: Track ==RED== signals per endpoint, backed by structured logs and traces.
Alert on **p95/p99** latency, not averages
Log JSON with `request_id`, no secrets
Add saturation: CPU, DB connections, queue depth

blocks.q: Q46. What is the difference between REST, GraphQL and gRPC?
a_bullets: All expose an API, differing in shape, transport and typing.
REST: HTTP resources, easy to cache
GraphQL: one endpoint, client picks fields
gRPC: binary Protobuf, HTTP/2, fast internally

blocks.q: Q47. How do you scale an API to handle millions of requests per day?
a_bullets: Go ==stateless==, scale out behind a load balancer, unblock the database.
Cache hot reads in Redis or CDN
Read replicas; shard for writes
Slow work onto a **queue**

blocks.q: Q48. How would you design a URL shortener API?
a_bullets: Map a ==short code== to the long URL; redirect on lookup.
Code = base62 of unique ID
Cache hot codes; reads dwarf writes
**302** for click counts

blocks.q: Q49. How would you design a notification or payment API?
a_bullets: Reply ==202== fast, queue the work, report status later.
**Idempotency-Key** on every POST
States: pending, sent, failed
Webhooks or polling for status

blocks.q: Q50. How do you handle partial failures, timeouts and retries between services?
a_bullets: Set a ==timeout== on every call, retry only idempotent requests, stop calling failing services.
Backoff plus **jitter**
Circuit breaker fails fast
Cap retries; fall back to cache

items: ==Errors==: one JSON shape with code and message

blocks.title: INTERVIEW TAKEAWAY:
blocks.text: Name the trade-off, then pick: safe methods, cursor paging, idempotent retries.

caption.text:
50 API interview questions they will ask you. 🎯

If you're going for a backend or SDE role, the API round is coming. Interviewers keep returning to the same ground, so this carousel covers all of it, in handwritten notes you can read in a few minutes.

What's inside:
📌 REST fundamentals and HTTP methods
📌 Status codes and HTTP headers
📌 Authentication basics, JWT and OAuth 2.0
📌 CORS and API security
📌 Pagination and filtering
📌 Rate limiting and throttling
📌 Caching and API gateways
📌 Idempotency and webhooks
📌 Versioning, file uploads and error handling
📌 Testing and monitoring
📌 Scalability and real-world design scenarios

Every page gives you three or four questions with short answers, key points and a quick visual. A cheatsheet at the end covers the last-minute revision.

Which of these questions do you find hardest? Tell me in the comments 👇

Save this for your next interview and send it to the friend who is prepping with you.

Comment “api” to get all the answers as a PDF.
